main_point.en: God desires mercy and goodness over rituals and laws.

christ_connection.en: l God’s mercy allowed His Son, Jesus, to die on the cross for humanity’s sin. We have always missed the mark of God’s holy standards of the law. But through Christ, we are rescued from the penalty of death because of His love and goodness.

content.en:
1 At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. 
2 But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” 
3 He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: 
4 how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? 
5 Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? 
6 I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. 
7 And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. 
8 For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.”

9 He went on from there and entered their synagogue. 
10 And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”—so that they might accuse him. 
11 He said to them, “Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? 
12 Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” 
13 Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. 
14 But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
Leaders: God values your love and devotion above your works. Let that truth give you rest.

“Jesus regularly highlighted a pharisaical neglect of Scripture as opposed to their conformity to tradition. In defense of his disciples’ behavior, Jesus cited the example of David in 1 Samuel 21:1-9, when he fled from Saul to the city of Nob, where the tabernacle was kept at the time. There David and his men ate the consecrated bread that was set apart for the priests to eat after it had been brought to the Lord as an offering (Lev. 24:8-9). Jesus was not citing a specific Old Testament quote in 12:5, but he was making a general observation. Throughout the Old Testament law, the Lord prescribed work for the priests on the Sabbath to facilitate the worship of others (Num. 28:9-10), and yet the priests were never declared guilty for such practices. Jesus argued that—based on those two examples and based on the fact that he himself, the architect of the temple and the one for whose worship the temple existed—he was ‘greater than the temple’ (12:6).”⁶

“Here Jesus used the quote to correct their misconception regarding the priority of mercy (the true spirit of the Sabbath law) over the letter of the law. God’s command to observe the Sabbath is an expression of mercy, recognizing the limits of the human makeup, and requiring us to care for the bodies and minds he has entrusted to us. The Pharisees had actually demeaned the Sabbath by robbing it of its ‘rest’ and weighting it with overwhelming religious requirements. This is what Jesus meant in Mark 2:27 when he said, ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.’ So mercy is wrapped up in the heart of the Sabbath law.”’⁷

“The fury of the Pharisees as they plotted to ‘destroy him’ was their own unintentional acknowledgment of Jesus’s complete moral victory over them. He contended for the value of a man and for the lawfulness of doing ‘good’ (kalos means what is proper) at any time, while they contended for the observance of a day. In effect, Jesus placed the love commandment above the Sabbath. Unable to meet him even on their own ground, they resorted to external force, the persecutor’s unwitting confession of defeat.”⁸

As Jesus taught and performed miracles, He repeatedly encountered conflict with the Jewish religious leaders of the day—scribes, Pharisees, and Sadducees. The Pharisees had burdened Israel with traditions and rules, but Jesus intended to bring rest (Matt. 11:28-30). Matthew 12 begins with accusations against Jesus and His disciples for violating the Sabbath. In the Old Testament, God gave the law to Israel to reveal sin and highlight the need for a Savior. The law was never intended to save Israel but rather pointed to the time when the “offspring” (Gen. 3:15) would come (Gal. 2:16; 3:19-26). The fourth commandment is to keep the Sabbath day holy, or set apart, meaning that Israel would work six days and rest one Ex. 20:8-11). God gave the Sabbath so that Israel might rest and remember the creation account and the origin story of Israel—so that the people could reflect on God’s faithfulness. Over the years, the Pharisees added very detailed rules for how to keep the Sabbath, most of which went much further than what God commanded. This distortion of the Sabbath meant that Jesus had to help Israel understand that the true intention of the Sabbath was to bring rest, not burden, just as He invited the crowd to find in Him (Matt. 11:28-30).

Mercy refers to God’s compassion and is often expressed in God’s withholding something, such as punishment for sin (Eph. 2:4-5; Titus 3:5). Both mercy and grace are undeserved, meaning humanity can do nothing to earn God’s mercy and grace. If one could, then it would no longer be the free gift of mercy or grace.

HEAVENLY FATHER, MAY OUR STUDENTS UNDERSTAND THE DEPTH OF YOUR MERCY THROUGH THE SACRIFICE OF YOUR SON. HOLY SPIRIT, OPEN OUR STUDENTS’ EYES AND EARS AS THEY ENCOUNTER YOUR MERCY IN YOUR WORD. HELP US WALK IN OBEDIENCE IN LOVING OUR NEIGHBOR AS OURSELVES.

The Pharisees created bizarre Sabbath rules, such as forbidding spitting on the ground (it could disturb soil, considered “plowing”), banning women from looking into a mirror (they might pull out a gray hair, considered “work”), and prohibiting wearing shoes with nails (an unnecessary burden).⁹

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You'll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for students to connect more to the lesson as they connect to the topic and to one another.

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: Are you naturally a rule-follower? Why or why not?
When a line or boundary is defined, how quickly do you go to the edge without technically breaking it? Why?
Which of your parents’ or guardians’ rules do you not understand the reason behind them?

content.en: Some environments have more rules than others, like school or airport security. Rules can feel like a burden or an inconvenience. We often choose which ones we’re willing to follow and which ones to ignore. When it comes to following Jesus, His commands aren’t a burden. They lead to meaningful life!

cultural_connection.en: Does our culture celebrate getting revenge or showing mercy? The world is slow to praise mercy and quick to reward harsh online comments, stories of revenge, and people getting what they deserve. This mentality can shape how we respond to offense, but this is not the way of the gospel. We’ve all made mistakes; we’ve all sinned and fallen short of God’s standard (Rom. 3:23). But in the face of all our failures, God shows us mercy—forgiveness instead of the punishment we deserve. The core of the gospel message is that sinners are not given what they deserve (death) but are given what they could never earn (salvation; Eph. 2:4-5). When you believe in this gospel, you’re no longer conformed to culture but transformed in your mind (Rom. 12:2). The more we dwell on the mercy that has been given to us through Jesus Christ, the more we grow in our ability to show mercy to others. Mercy transforms our minds and hearts so that we carry mercy to others in an effort to reveal Jesus to the world.

question.en: How do you rest? What mattered most about Sabbath to Pharisees?

answer.en: Some of us rest by sleeping in, taking time off work, or going for a walk. Resting the way God commands is intentional—obediently pausing to depend on God and to reflect on His faithfulness. The Pharisees accused the disciples of working on the Sabbath for picking grain to eat! Their interpretation of God’s law clouded their vision; rules and traditions mattered more than human needs. The Pharisees strictly enforced rules, burdening the people with standards they could never keep. They believed keeping these rules proved their righteousness, but Jesus reminded them that the Sabbath was a gift of rest, not a burdensome test.

question.en: Read Hosea 6:6. What do you think it means that God desires “steadfast love” (or mercy), not sacrifice?

answer.en: The Pharisees believed sacrifices and rule-following made them righteous, or made their hearts right with God. But they had it backwards; they failed to see that religious practice without mercy misses God’s heart. What God desires most is justice, love, and humility (Mic. 6:6-8); He wants not sacrifice, but obedience (1 Sam. 15:22) and service (Deut. 10:12-13). Jesus perfectly revealed God’s heart and rightly interpreted the law. Good works must flow from a surrendered heart. We can’t keep the law; religious duty can’t save us and means nothing unless we have a relationship with Jesus.

question.en: What does Jesus mean by claiming He is “Lord of the Sabbath”? Should Christians observe the Sabbath today?

answer.en: When Jesus corrected the Pharisees, He didn’t challenge the Sabbath itself but how the people had interpreted it. Jesus, the Son of Man, is the “Lord of the Sabbath,” which means He has the authority to define the Sabbath. As the Son of Man, Jesus established that He was God’s Son—that He is God! He has authority over all things, including the Sabbath. Jesus reminded them that the Sabbath was a gift of mercy, not a burden. If we come to the Bible as the Pharisees did and try to find life and rest in the words, we are crushed by rules and burdens (John 5:39), but if we come to Jesus, the Word of God (John 1:1), we find eternal life and permanent rest in Him (Matt. 11:28-30). He kept the law when we couldn’t. The Sabbath was a good gift for God’s people because it pointed them to their Creator. But Jesus reminded the Pharisees, and us today, that the Sabbath was made for people and not the other way around (Mark 2:27-28). God’s command to rest applies to us because He designed us with the need to rest (Mark 6:31), and as we do, we should remember who God is—our Creator who gives us life and rest in Jesus.

question.en: What point did Jesus make in the example of a sheep falling into a pit on the Sabbath?

answer.en: Jesus cut through the Pharisees’ ongoing debate concerning how much one could help others before breaking the Sabbath and pointed to what He desires most: showing mercy by doing what is good. Jesus reframed the Sabbath as a day for doing good instead of a day for avoiding work. Imagine walking down a road and hearing a dog yelping for help. Would you help? The Pharisees’ answer to this question wasn’t so easy because of their misunderstanding of the Sabbath. Jesus elevated the meaning of the Sabbath by showing that God’s heart is always to help those in need. Jesus made the same point in the parable of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37). When we do good to others, we fulfill the law (Matt. 12:12). Jesus wasn’t breaking the law because God said mercy is better than sacrifice or empty rule-following (Hos. 6:6).

question.en: Why did the Pharisees plot Jesus’s death?

answer.en: The Pharisees cared more about rules than helping those in need. Jesus responded to the man with a paralyzed hand by reaching out and healing him, resulting in the Pharisees plotting His death! The Pharisees loved to debate interpretations of the law and legal cases, but they wouldn’t kill someone over a difference of opinion only. They clearly understood that Jesus was claiming to be the Messiah by referring to Himself as the “Son of Man,” a Messianic term. He claimed the authority to forgive sins! During Roman occupation, the Jews were unable to condemn someone to death (John 18:31), so they had to carefully plot out Jesus’s destruction.

question.en: Why do we struggle to love others the way Jesus did? How are we sometimes more like Pharisees?

answer.en: Jesus met combative, argumentative people, but instead of retaliating, He repaid evil with good (Rom. 12:17-21). Jesus loved the man with a withered hand by healing him, and He loved the Pharisees by speaking truth. We often struggle to love others. Like the Pharisees, we’re blind to those who need help, more eager to win arguments or to point out sin. Jesus loves by showing compassion to those in need. He calls us to love others by sacrificially serving them (John 15:12-13). Our natural desire can be to lash out in anger at enemies, block them, or gossip about them; God says we must love our neighbor as ourselves (Lev. 19:18). The law reminds us of God’s mercy, which fuels our desire to love others.

question.en: How can you show mercy to someone in your life who doesn’t deserve it?

answer.en: Is anyone too evil, too sinful, or too difficult to receive God’s mercy and love? We don’t see evidence for this in the Gospels. In Jesus’s many rebukes to the scribes and Pharisees, He taught them the way of God’s kingdom—that God is willing to save anyone. Jesus knew one of the twelve disciples, Judas, would eventually betray Him, but He still showed Judas mercy and washed his feet (John 13). Jesus revealed the grace and mercy of God perfectly (Heb. 1:3), and He invites us to follow His steps—to love one another. Is there someone you actively avoid? Anyone you’re paying back with evil for the evil they did to you? Anyone you feel is too sinful to hear the gospel? Because of sin, getting revenge feels natural, but when we follow Jesus, we are new creations. By the power of the Holy Spirit, we can be like Jesus and choose to show mercy in the face of evil. God doesn’t give us what we deserve (Rom. 6:23), so may we be quick to show mercy to others in the same way God has shown us mercy.

content.en:
Have you ever had to follow a rule that you just didn’t understand or agree with? Immediately obeying rules is often the right response and shows a humble heart. But sometimes, not understanding the reason for a rule can eventually lead to confusion; because we don’t understand the point of the rule, we become bitter about following it.

The Pharisees, or religious leaders, became confused about the Sabbath and began to add their own restrictions to God’s command; even more, they didn’t understand God’s heart behind the command for the Sabbath. God gave the Sabbath command to Moses and the Israelites as a good gift. They were to set aside a day to rest in God and worship Him, instead of going about their normal work. The Pharisees warped the Sabbath day into a burden by adding extra restrictions to it. They focused so much on what they were doing and whether or not they were breaking a command that they lost focus on God. Jesus explained that the Sabbath was never meant to be a burden but a day of worshipful rest. The Sabbath is still God’s good gift for us! In taking a day from our busy schedules to focus on God, we imitate God’s rest from creation. We are recharged and refocused—more equipped to live out the Christian life. Jesus, as Lord of the Sabbath, reminds us that the Sabbath was for us, not to focus only on ourselves, but on Christ and what He has done to accomplish our eternal rest. It is a day of physical rest that points to our spiritual rest. Regardless of what cultures says, Sabbath is still a holy day.

question.en: Do you have a set day or time during the week to rest and focus on the Lord? What can you do to free up more time for holy, intentional rest?
Why is the Sabbath a good gift for us? How does it reflect God’s work and rest?

prayer.en: Father, thank You for rest. We were made to find our greatest joy and peace in You and not in ourselves or in our work. Help us to remember the Sabbath day and to resist the lie that we’re too busy to spend time with You.

content.en: The odds are high that someone has sinned against you. This may have made you upset or angry. When this happens, we often feel justified in our anger. Surely God feels anger over sin and injustice. Christians should feel anger over sin as well because it causes harm (Ps. 5:5-6). However, sin should also make us sorrowful because Jesus gave His life for it. God’s wrath and anger toward sin is righteous and holy, but it mingles with His own grief toward sin as well (Gen. 6:6; Matt. 23:37-39). In today’s passage, Christ grieved because the religious leaders’ hearts were so hardened that they couldn’t see someone in need of mercy and healing. The Lord desires the salvation of all people, and though He is rightly angry with sin, He is also sorrowful over how sin has infected His good creation, especially human beings who bear His image (2 Pet. 3:9). God’s response to sin, therefore, should form our response to sin. God feels anger and sorrow over sin, but ultimately, He shows us mercy when we call on Him for salvation. Though sin can make us angry at times, our frustration must point toward the real enemy—Satan. We should feel sorrow for the sinner, which leads to mercy and the desire for all sinners to repent. We must boldly approach the lost with the truth of the gospel. We must call sin exactly what it is! When we skip this step, we cheapen the gospel. We cheapen Jesus’s sacrifice. But we must also share the love of Christ from a heart that desires for others to be saved. When we see sin in the world, may we remember who we were before Christ found us. May we compassionately approach the lost world with the transforming truth of the gospel. Our love for lost people and our desire for them to share in our hope should triumph over our anger at their sin. God’s love for us triumphed over sin when He sent Christ to take our punishment. May we follow His example as we help others know the way to freedom and forgiveness.

question.en: Why do we often act more like the religious leaders in this passage than like Jesus?
How can we seek to be more like Jesus in our feelings and actions toward those who don’t know Him?

prayer.en: Father, even though You are rightly angry with our sin, You show us mercy and love. Help us to love lost people and to speak the gospel with boldness.

content.en:
A lot of life seems to depend on how well we can perform. If you play sports, you are judged on how well you can play, how fast you can run, or how accurately you can throw. In school, you earn grades based on your skill in certain subjects. This performance-driven mindset can easily creep into how we view our relationship with God. Our relationship with God and the efforts we make to grow can unintentionally become just another thing we do in our busy lives. Prayer, Bible reading, and going to church become boxes that we check off to make us feel like we are being “good Christians.” But is this how God wants us to live our lives? Thankfully, no.

God wants our love and devotion before He wants our good works. In fact, our good works are like filthy rages when they don’t flow from a heart redeemed by Christ (Isa. 64:6). We do good works, not to make God love us more, but in response to the fact that He has already loved us. How often are we like the Israelites, who thought their burnt offerings and sacrifices would satisfy God, even though their hearts did not love Him? Or the religious leaders, who put their own rules above God’s intention for the law and accused Jesus’s disciples of sinning when they picked grain on the Sabbath? If we’re honest, we are often tempted to see our works or “goodness” as a way of earning God’s love—as a way of showing others how “good” we are. The truth is that no one is good or righteous (Rom. 3:10-12), and our good works don’t make us deserving of God’s love or make Him love us more. He already loved us before we could choose to love Him in return. God first desires our love, not our works. Only when we love Him deeply can we then serve Him rightly.

question.en: Have you ever done good works to earn praise or to impress people? Why is this a problem?
How can the gospel free us to do good works without feeling like we must work to earn God’s love?

prayer.en: Father, thank You for grace. We could never earn or deserve Your love. Help us to remember the gospel and to love You in return—with our whole hearts, hoping only in Christ and not our works.

content.en:
When Jesus healed a person on the Sabbath, many religious leaders accused Him of breaking the command not to work on the Sabbath. By the time Jesus came to earth, the religious leaders had added extra rules to God’s law. Perhaps they thought they were being obedient, ensuring that the law would not be broken by giving very specific rules to follow. However, they ended up missing God’s point entirely. The religious leaders had forgotten that God gave them the law, not only as a guide for right living, but also as a means for revealing His character to all people. We can’t do away with the law, but we shouldn't add to it or see it simply as a list of rules to follow. And if we’re honest, many of us have viewed God’s commands this way and failed to see that His commands are like a gift, guiding us to know Him and to live for Him.

When Jesus healed on the Sabbath, He didn’t violate the command to rest on the Sabbath. Instead, He fulfilled the command for the Sabbath to be a holy day, set apart to worship God and rest. His healing on the Sabbath reflected the purpose of the law itself—to allow us to see who God is and to help us be more like Him. Jesus is the only One who followed the law perfectly. He didn’t bend the rules; He showed us God’s heart for His commands. He fulfilled the law. Jesus showed us what following and living out God’s commands looks like. The religious leaders didn’t understand the law because they missed God’s heart revealed in the law. Jesus Christ, God in the flesh, lovingly showed us the intention of the law. He showed us both the heart of God in the law and the way to apply it in real life.

question.en: When you think about God’s commands, specifically the Ten Commandments, do you see them as simply a list of rules or as something else?
What are some ways you can see more of God’s character in His commands to us?

prayer.en: Father, thank You for showing us who You are in Your commands to us. Thank You that Jesus fulfilled the law for us so that we can see Your heart, not with anxiety but because of the freedom we have in Christ.

content.en:
Rules, rules, and more rules. Our days can feel weighted down with rules at school, rules at home, rules in our groups and activities. If we’re honest, we can feel like following Jesus is a list of rules too. Want to hear some good news? The Bible never supports this mentality. Following the Lord is so much more than following rules.

Jesus never taught that His disciples should be burdened by His commands. Just before the passage in this week’s lesson, Jesus taught that anyone with a heavy burden should come to Him and receive rest. Jesus offers us rest because He fulfilled the law for us and is able to forgive our sins. The heavy burden of the law was placed on His shoulders, the only One sinless and worthy enough to carry it. Because Jesus fulfilled the law perfectly, He then could offer Himself as a sacrifice for the sins of all who could not keep the law perfectly—for all of us. Therefore, if we place our faith in Jesus, then we receive rest from the unbearable weight of having to follow the law to be in right standing with God. Instead, because we are in Christ, we receive His righteousness and are saved and accepted by God, only by grace through faith. We are freed from the burden of the law, and instead, we are able to rest in the fact that Christ’s sacrifice is enough to save us when we call on Him in faith. This doesn’t mean we do away with the law and not seek to obey it. Actually, we are gifted with the Holy Spirit, who frees us and empowers us to obey! We seek to imitate Jesus in all that we do, while also realizing that if and when we fail to do it perfectly, we can repent and find forgiveness in Him who alone is perfect.

question.en: What are some ways that following Jesus feels like a burden or a list of rules to you?
How does the truth that Jesus has fulfilled the law perfectly empower us to follow Him joyfully and without feeling weighed down?

prayer.en: Father, thank You that Christ has fulfilled the law. Help me to come to Jesus for all of my needs and to follow Him with my whole heart, not with anxiety but because of the freedom I have in Him.
